He cut Smiley Loose, Loose too. Bobby Mitchell, he cut everybody loose.
Yeah, well, Bobby told me that, uh, he, he had a suit against Lou Chez. Because he, he was, he should have gotten some money from the Wheel record. I remember there, Wheel someday.

Well, I imagine he should have gotten it. Uh, see, uh, what, what, what was happening, uh, there were so many different artists and so many people making records. And, uh, well, he just couldn't keep up with what was going on, you know. So, man, just decided to clean up the house and just cut everybody loose. And, uh, Bobby Mitchell recorded that number. It's true. Yeah. And, Roy Brown also recorded it for the same label for Imperial, too. Well, the guy from Baton Rouge wrote it.
Yeah.

And, David Thalemur put his name on it. Yeah. Bobby Mitchell's name is not, there's nowhere on that record. So, maybe, maybe, maybe, uh, he should, I don't know, he could get some money. You know, you know, Fats Domino did it, too.
Yeah, he sure did.
And then Fats's name was on it.
Yeah, Fats, yeah.
Fats, Fats did it, too. Fats and Bartholomew, in fact.
Fats did it, too.
Fats did it, too. Fats did it.
With the, uh, Smyler Lewis and P. Eynakin. D&Anakin, Smarter was on it.
Yeah, Smiley wrote how he gave him.
Dave was out of his hands on it?
Dave was out of his hands on it? Dave was out of his hands on everything that was released on Imperial. Everybody records for Imperial. Dave wouldn't record it unless you put your name on it.
What kind of guy was that going to call me?
Just like I said, just like I just said, he was arrogant and he said, well, if you want to record, I'm going to get half of it.
He would tell you that before you signed the contract. He would say, if you signed this contract, I just want you to know I'm taking half.
Yeah, that's the kind of guy he was.
Everybody would still sign?
Well, everybody wanted to make a record. That's the way it was.
Imperial was the biggest label in New Orleans back then.
Yeah, Imperial had more artists than anybody. That's the way it was.
What kind of business man was Sam Montel? Who wanted to take care of this man?

I don't know. Because I didn't have a chance to be around him too very much. Except for the time that I worked for him. Well, maybe once or twice. At the nightclub and all that, at this community center in Baton Rouge. We worked for him quite often. Maybe, maybe, uh, once a month for maybe six months, I'd say. And, uh, well, he had to treat us, honestly, then because, well, the crowd spoke for itself. You know, like, we go in places, we see, we see a gymnasium full of people. He had to pay us, you know, and, and wasn't no three or four dollars, you know. He, uh, he, uh.
Is that the same thing about Johnny Vinson?
Johnny Vinson, I mean, Johnny, Johnny Vinson. Well.
One of many who stood in the shadow of Johnny Vinson. Yeah.

I can't say nothing good about Johnny Vinson. Nothing. Unless I say about Johnny Vinson, it's better off my feet. Because I can't say nothing good about him. They don't say nothing bad about the person. Don't say nothing bad. So I won't say nothing at all.
You can't say something good about somebody. Don't say anything at all. Right. But Johnny Vinson's case sometimes should make an exception.
Man, Johnny Vinson is something else.
He tried to pull every kind of trick in a book just to make a doll on him.
I know you messed up Uriah Smith. I guess he would've, uh, probably, probably did a good job of messing around. And I don't see, uh, how Jimmy Clanton got hung up with him in the first place.
Well, Clanton had, uh, Clanton was like cute. I mean, like, a lot. He was only like 19 when he started.
Yeah. Yeah, he was, yeah.
He saw the contracts and he didn't really know what he was getting into. But he did see some money. He did see some money or something.
Well.
I'm sure of that.
He probably made money mostly on a personal appearance or something. Yeah.
Yeah, I don't think he made too much on the records. And that's, and that's from Johnny Vinson.

So that became his boy, and that was his boy at the point. Yeah, well, yeah. Cause he really, I think he really thought he put a lot of time into the class. I know he did. And because of it, a lot of his other artists suffered. You know, Neely Smith suffered and a lot of other people. Suffered. You only did that one record before he put you out of the day? Yeah. Yeah.
I, uh, that's the, that was the only thing I did. And, uh, I, uh, did this, this, uh, this, this album, you know. And Jimmy Plannan was on there, you know.
What's some of the big places that you played when you were on tour?
Like, did you play like the big theaters of Beasts, like the Howard Theater in Washington?
No, uh, I played, uh, the Plaza, uh, New York. Plaza? Mm-hmm. And, um, Gleason, Cleveland. Gleason?
Yeah.
This was a long time ago. Yeah. Um.
How about Chicago?

I was trying to think of some of the places in Chicago. Cause I played in Chicago many times. I don't remember. I don't, I, I don't, I really, I don't. You didn't think I played there? Yeah, it was, but I don't think, I don't think I played there. But, uh, well, there's so many different places to play, you know. Well, I don't, I don't remember, uh, all the places I played. But I do remember being there. I remember playing there. What do you remember about Guitar Slim? Yeah, uh-huh.
Yeah, I remember, he killed himself. You know, Guitar Slim had a Cadillac. Yeah. Yeah.
He was driving down LaSalle Street. And at the time, there was, uh, there was, there was, there was fixing LaSalle Street. They were doing something.
They were doing something.
They was making this curve where LaSalle goes into Simon Bollower.
Right.

And they had the street kind of barricaded there. And, uh, he ran into, into the barricades, went to the hospital. You know, it was hurt, you know. And, you know. And he had the street kind of barricaded there. And, uh, he ran into, into the barricades, went to the hospital. You know, it was hurt, you know. He had him wrecked, drunk. He had him wrecked and all that. So, he was under the doctor's treatment. And the doctor had fluid, uh, on his, on his lungs. Something, something happened to him. Anyway, he was supposed to go back to the doctor every so often. Instead of going back to the doctor and taking it easy, he leaves. He leaves town. Going out there, supposed to be making money.
He was a pretty heavy drinker, wasn't he?
Yeah. Oh, yeah. It gets us slim as a natural clown. And, uh, so, he just got sick and died.
Well, that's the host's way of living. He never, he never stopped. Yep.
They tell me he used to be a block away sometime playing the guitar.

Yeah, and he had a, he had a long chord on his guitar. And, uh, one night, one night we played, uh, we played in Edgar, uh, on the river road. Yeah. And, uh, guitar slam was playing, and, uh, he went out, out of the dance hall, and got under a car, playing, with guitar. And we had to come get him. He got stuck and couldn't get out. He was under the car.
He got under, I don't know how in the world he did it.
He was still playing the guitar. He was still playing the guitar as long as he could. He couldn't get out, so we had to go get him.
Did you, uh, piano, you played piano, did you, did you, uh, listen to anybody? Like, did, did you, uh, try to play like Professor Long here?
I never tried to play like anybody. I just, I just liked to play piano, and I just played. I never really, uh, idolized anybody, really.
Do you remember the, do you remember the chords to, uh, Ico Ico, on the music one? Do you remember?

Mmm, mmm. What G was that? It was in G, and it was, uh, G, G, G, D. G? G, G, G, G, and G, D. That's all. G, mmm, Tynakin, Fifth. That was it. That was it. That's all. It was only two changes, you know.
Who were some of the other good piano players in the city, way back, in the fifties? There was one guy that could really play, um, Santee, I think his name was Santee.

No. No, no. No, no, no. No, no. No, no. Oh, God dog, what's his name? No. No, no. I remember him. I remember him. I remember him. The first time I heard him play, I heard him play Caravan. And I really, I really, I really, uh, blocked his style. Um, Santee, I think his name was Santee. I think his name was Santee. Santiago? No. No, no. Oh, God dog, what's his name? I remember him. I remember him. I remember him. The first time I heard him play, I heard him play Caravan. And I really, I really, uh, blocked his style of playing. Uh, Paul Gaten was, now he was, he was good piano player, Paul Gaten. And I think Paul Gaten played on a lot of, uh, uh, uh, this guy named Play Guitar, what's his name? Uh, Chuck Berry. I think Paul Gaten played on a lot of Chuck Berry's numbers.
Yeah, he worked for London Chess.
Yeah. And, uh, uh, uh, Salvador Duce. Yeah, Salvador, yeah. We went to school together.
Where's he at now? I don't know. Did you know we Willie Wayne? Did you travel in the mood? James Wayne. James Wayne? Mm-hmm.
What, to get back to your family, did, uh, what did your father do for living?
He was just common labor.
He was a labor?
Mm-hmm.
Anything special?
Nope. Did any of your family play music right? Uh-uh. Where you working at now? At the Fairmont Hotel. Oh, the Roosevelt, yeah.
Yeah. The man said he don't want the Roosevelt on nothing he owns.
The man bought the Roosevelt. And changed the name of it.
Fairmont. Fairmont. No, it's just the Fairmont.
It was the Fairmont. It was for a while. It was a Fairmont Roosevelt, but then he took the Roosevelt off too.
I don't know. I think his name is, uh, let's see what's his name. Oh boy.
Oh, mm.
Oh boy. I can't think of his name.
I can't think of his name.
Oh boy. Oh, no. I don't know. I can't think of his name.
Oh, no. I don't know. I can't think of his name.
Well, I don't know.
Yeah, I think this guy is from Los Angeles. Yeah, it's a Fairmont. Yeah, it's a Fairmont. He just changed. He took the Fairmont.
He took the Roosevelt off too. I don't know. Who's the guy with him for?

I think his name is, uh, let's see what's his name. Oh boy. Oh, mm. I can't think of his name. Oh, well. I don't know. Yeah, I think this guy is from Los Angeles. Or San Francisco, I rather. Oh, yeah.
He's from San Francisco. He's got a hotel out there. He has four.
He has a Fairmont. He has one in Atlanta, one in Dallas, one in New Orleans, one in San Francisco.
Yeah, because there's one in San Francisco. I think it's called Fairmont or something. He's probably trying to keep the names and say it was. Yeah. When did you get married?
Mmm, 53.
What was your wife's name?
Gwendolyn. That was my first wife. Gwendolyn.
What was her last time of death breakup?

I'm not too young. No. We both were pretty young, so we never tried to make anything up. It was really... I was 19, 18, something like that. And she was about 16, so... When did you get married again? In... 50... 58.
58, I think.

58. Because I was older then. I guess I was... I know I was older. I guess I was a little wiser. But it didn't really matter too much. Do you remember, is your wife still living? Yeah. My mother lived in San Francisco. I was a little wiser. I think I was a little wiser. I guess I was a little wiser. I guess I was a little wiser. I guess I was a little wiser. I guess I was a little wiser. I guess I was a little wiser. But it didn't really matter too much.
Is your wife still living or.... Yeah. My mother....
Oh, that was my mother.
I don't know where she is now.
Did anybody get in trouble with your band or the police? No. I mean, did any groups when you were on the road have trouble getting black and white that we all get in trouble?
No, that's the only time that it would happen when I got hurt.
What, Rabinac was what you did?

No. Nope. You know, what I really think happened, the police stopped me and said I was speeding and I was drunk and they took me to jail. But what I really think it was, this happened in 1963. It was during the time they were having these Freedom Rides. And I was going to Monroe. This happened in North Louisiana. And I was going up there and I was pulling the trail. I had a trail on the back of my car. And I guess police must have thought we was coming up there to try to create some kind of disturbance. So it was about 11 o'clock in the morning when it happened. Oh, wasn't it night? No, it wasn't in the morning.
Oh, that kind of makes sense. And you know, you can think of somebody being drunk and speeding later at night.

Yeah, see, this is what happened. See, we left home, we left New Orleans. And the jail was, that happened on a Tuesday. And the jail was for 9 o'clock that Tuesday night. And we was in Monroe. We would have been up there for 11.30 that day. We could have stayed there all day, you know. We left home early that morning. Because nobody had anything to do. I said, okay, now let's leave early. Like maybe around 5, 5, 6 o'clock in the morning. And we could take our time, you know. Drive slow. You wouldn't have to worry about rushing. You know, we have a whole lot of time. So everybody agreed. So we just left, really. We left something like, like 5, I think around 5 o'clock, 4.30, 5 o'clock in the morning. We left. And we was in Monroe around 11 o'clock, you know. That's what happened. And we were.
There were more people than you in the car.
Yeah. It was, we had two cars and, you know. Had five, let's see, three, four, five, five people in my car.
So when the cops stopped you, it wasn't just you. I mean, he was out there, he was out there who bought the cops.
They had five people in my car and six people in the other car.
Was there much, were many of the musicians in New Orleans involved with drugs and all?
I don't know. I don't know, really.
Some of them got in trouble with their laws, but Mac and James Booker. I don't know if Mac was involved.
Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah. Booker was, yeah, Booker was in a whole lot of trouble at one time. And I know Mac, Mac was too. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
I don't know about Walter.
I know him, but I wasn't too familiar with him.
You ever think about getting back into it? No. The sound has changed too much.

Well, no. I think it would be just a waste of time, a big waste of time. I don't think there would be any point in trying to go back into it. Well, I guess the sound had changed, but that wouldn't mean anything. I think I can handle myself well enough to change too. But I wouldn't want to get back into it. It just seemed like it would be such a great, not a loss, but it would require too much of my time and too much of a sacrifice on my part. And this is something I wouldn't want to do. I couldn't afford to do it because I got to live. I didn't mind being out of a job for a couple of months at that time when I was really into it when I first started because I had my mother and father to depend on. But now I have somebody depending on me so I can't afford to do that.
How many kids you got?
Two. My oldest daughter is getting married Saturday.
What's her son?
Andre.
Bernie Depp and Andre. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

segments.title: Interview opening, date and birth in New Orleans
segments.summary: Date of the interview is settled; Crawford gives his birthday as October 12, 1934, in New Orleans.

segments.title: Schooling, symphony concerts and growing interest in music
segments.summary: He says weekly school symphony concerts grew on him; he names his schools and that he is an only child of Mary and James.

segments.title: Church choir and teaching himself piano around age 12
segments.summary: His father sang in the church choir; Crawford taught himself piano with friends, not learning from anyone in particular.

segments.title: Growing up on South Robertson in the Garden District
segments.summary: He describes the neighborhood he lived in until about age 22.

segments.title: First band in high school and radio spot on Dr. Daniel's show
segments.summary: In 1951 he formed an eight-piece school band that began at the Shadowland and played Saturday radio on WMRY.

segments.title: Members of the school band
segments.summary: He lists the players: Big Boy Myles, Nolan Blackwell, Alfred Bernard, David Lastie, Warren Miles, Alfred Woodard, Bannister, Edgar Miles and drummer Eric Warner.

segments.title: How the band got the name Shawee
segments.summary: The band's name came from a theme number the group made up, which Dr. Daniel mentioned in his newspaper column.

segments.title: Early record with Big Boy Myles singing and Crawford crying
segments.summary: They discuss an early record where Big Boy Myles sang lead while Crawford did the crying.

segments.title: Still in school, the band as a bunch of kids
segments.summary: He was still in school and living with his parents at about 16; the drummer was the youngest at 14.

segments.title: From Shawee to Sugar Boy and the Cane Cutters
segments.summary: The name was cut down on the contract, he signed as leader under his childhood nickname, and Chess added Cane Cutters.

segments.title: Meeting Leonard Chess and trips to Chicago
segments.summary: He says Leonard Chess was involved with his sessions, and he went to Chicago but did not record there.

segments.title: Writing Jock-A-Mo and its success in New York
segments.summary: He wrote the song from Mardi Gras Indian ideas at 19, and its success led to a New York trip needing special club permission.

segments.title: Who played on the Chess records
segments.summary: He tries to recall sidemen including Snooks Eaglin, Big Boy Myles, David Lastie and a forgotten saxophonist.

segments.title: Recording live in one take; David Lastie's sax solo
segments.summary: He sang and played piano live in one take; David Lastie took the solo and now plays with Frogman Henry.

segments.chapter: Touring, band and money in the 1950s-60s
segments.title: Royalties from Chess and signing a contract while underage
segments.summary: The second record made money; he bought suits and went to New York, and he should not have signed a contract at his age.

segments.chapter: Touring, band and money in the 1950s-60s
segments.title: Touring without a manager
segments.summary: He booked his own tours across the South and to Chicago, and says he had trouble on the road.

segments.chapter: Touring, band and money in the 1950s-60s
segments.title: Police beating in Monroe in 1963
segments.summary: In 1963 on the way to a job he was hit on the head by police, was paralyzed and hospitalized; he lists his band members then.

segments.chapter: Touring, band and money in the 1950s-60s
segments.title: Smiley Lewis in the band and why he gave up the band
segments.summary: Smiley Lewis played guitar with his band and learned from the bassist; Crawford's band was praised but he could not afford to keep it.

segments.chapter: Touring, band and money in the 1950s-60s
segments.title: Leaving Chess and recording best work for Imperial
segments.summary: Contracts lapsed when sales faded; he made many records for Imperial which he considers his best.

segments.chapter: Touring, band and money in the 1950s-60s
segments.title: Clubs played in New Orleans in the 1950s
segments.summary: He names the Showboat on Bourbon Street, Pete's Paradise and Club Tijuana, and says he never played Robin Hood.

segments.chapter: Touring, band and money in the 1950s-60s
segments.title: Pay in the 1950s, five dollars for four hours
segments.summary: Gigs paid five or six dollars a piece; the whole band split five dollars after four hours.

segments.chapter: Touring, band and money in the 1950s-60s
segments.title: Being recorded unknowingly at WMRY for five dollars
segments.summary: His first record was cut at the radio station without his knowing it was a recording, paid five dollars and released without a contract.

segments.chapter: Touring, band and money in the 1950s-60s
segments.title: No royalties for Jock-A-Mo
segments.summary: He got nothing from the Dixie Cups' version because he was not credited as writer and it was never copyrighted.

segments.title: Playing with Tommy Ridgley and quitting in 1969
segments.summary: He disbanded in 1967, helped Tommy Ridgley on piano, and last played on New Year's night 1969.

segments.title: Peacock records and the other James Crawford
segments.summary: He discusses a 1963 Peacock record on which he was not the singer, and the Sugar Lumps.

segments.title: Session run by someone else; Don Robey holds back release
segments.summary: He recalls who ran the Peacock session and says Don Robey delayed release until he recovered, which never came.

segments.title: Imperial cutting artists loose and Bobby Mitchell's song credit
segments.summary: Lew Chudd released many artists from contracts; they discuss Bobby Mitchell's song and who got credit.

segments.title: Dave Bartholomew's demand for half and Imperial's dominance
segments.summary: Bartholomew required his name on records released on Imperial, the biggest New Orleans label.

segments.title: Baton Rouge promoter and Johnny Vincent's treatment of artists
segments.summary: He worked often for a Baton Rouge promoter and speaks harshly of Johnny Vincent and his handling of Jimmy Clanton.

segments.chapter: Piano, Guitar Slim and personal life
segments.title: Big venues played on tour
segments.summary: He played the Plaza in New York and places in Cleveland and Chicago but cannot recall them all.

segments.chapter: Piano, Guitar Slim and personal life
segments.title: Guitar Slim's accident, death and stunts
segments.summary: He tells how Guitar Slim wrecked his car, left town against doctor's orders and died, and the story of him playing under a car.

segments.chapter: Piano, Guitar Slim and personal life
segments.title: Piano influences and the chords to Jock-A-Mo
segments.summary: He never idolized anyone on piano, and the song had only two chords in G.

segments.chapter: Piano, Guitar Slim and personal life
segments.title: Other New Orleans pianists of the fifties
segments.summary: He recalls a pianist playing Caravan, Paul Gayten and Salvador Doucette.

segments.chapter: Piano, Guitar Slim and personal life
segments.title: Father's work and no musicians in the family
segments.summary: His father was a common laborer and no one else in the family played.

segments.chapter: Piano, Guitar Slim and personal life
segments.title: Where he works now and the Fairmont hotel name
segments.summary: Chat about his current job at the Fairmont, formerly the Roosevelt, and its owner.

segments.chapter: Piano, Guitar Slim and personal life
segments.title: Marriages in 1953 and 1958
segments.summary: He married Gwendolyn in 1953 when both were young and married again in 1958.

segments.title: Why the police stopped him: Freedom Rides and the trip to Monroe
segments.summary: He thinks police suspected the band of coming to cause disturbance during the Freedom Rides; they left early with two cars.

segments.title: Musicians and drug trouble
segments.summary: He says James Booker and Mac got in trouble with the law; he did not know others well.

segments.title: Why he will not return to music; his children
segments.summary: He sees returning as a waste of time and cannot afford it; he has two children and a daughter getting married.
